entry.title: 21 CFR Part 11 is where 'approve by email' shops quietly fail — a typed name is not a signature
entry.summary: The CAPA that taught me what an email isn't Two years ago I inherited a CAPA queue that included a finding from our prior notified body audit. The wording was polite but unambiguous: "The approval records for the post-market surveillance report could not be verified against a Part 11-compliant system." I went looking. The approval record was a four-message email thread. The approver had typed their name in a reply. The original report was an attachment that had since been edited and re-uploaded to the shared drive. The "signature" and the "record" had no binding I could demonstrate to an auditor — or to myself. That's the trap. "Approve by email" feels rigorous. Someone wrote a name. Someone replied "approved." There's a date. It looks like evidence. Under 21 CFR Part 11, it isn't. When an…

entry.summary: Follow-up work is the stuff that happens after the "real" task: chasing a reply, checking that a fix actually shipped, confirming that a request someone promised to handle got handled. entry.title: 4 Governance Rules for a Simple Node.js SaaS App Background Job Queue
entry.summary: Short answer: use a background job queue for outbound media webhook work, make every receiver idempotent, and reserve cron for scheduled enqueueing. The queue may deliver a standard message more than once; the design is correct only when the same logical delivery can be processed twice without producing two customer-visible effects. This is a governance decision, not a search for an “exactly once” checkbox. A media SaaS sending asset.ready, caption.updated, and license.expiring notifications across US and EU deployments has three different records in play: the application owns the event, the queue owns pending work, and the destination owns the effect. Confusing those records is how a retry policy turns into duplicate publication notices. Adopt the queue-and-worker design only with stable …

entry.title: Pin your relay config in ~/.claude/settings.json (no more export every time)
Debugging a relay API in Claude Code / Codex: 401 vs 404 vs 429
entry.summary: When you point Claude Code or Codex at a third-party relay and it errors, read the status code first — it tells you exactly what's wrong: 404 — wrong address. Usually the /v1 on base_url: Anthropic-compatible endpoints have no /v1 (Claude Code appends /v1/messages); OpenAI-compatible endpoints need /v1. 401 / 403 — auth failed. Key copied in full? Credit left? Model id in the station's list? Claude Code must use ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN (Bearer), not ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. 429 — the station is rate-limiting. Switch stations or wait; retrying just lengthens the queue. 400 / content blocked — upstream moderation. Retry in plain English/Chinese; if it keeps firing, switch stations. Keep a couple of stations registered so a single one rate-limiting never blocks you. List with tested dates: AI relay station list Signup links carry my referral param; strip ?aff= if you prefer.
